A free-chain counterexample to a Nash-intersection conjecture

Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X

22 October 2026 · Version 1.0.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23578599

Original abstract

We compute the intersection of the closed Nash sets of the complete family of prime divisors obtained by n successive free point blowups over (ℂ²,0), after fixing a prefix of k centers, where 2≤k<n. In suitable coordinates the intersection is {ord x≥⌈n/k⌉, ord y≥n}. For five blowups, fixing two or three centers gives the thresholds (3,5) or (2,5). Neither is q(1,j) for positive integers q,j. These examples disprove the specified-reference-multiple assertion in Conjecture 1 of Fernández de Bobadilla, Pe Pereira and Popescu-Pampu, under each contact and indexing convention explicitly treated here. The source's bare equivalence symbol is undefined and its indexing is inconsistent; no unique author-intended correction is asserted. The intersections are themselves maximal divisorial sets for other toric divisors. Thus the result does not disprove an assertion allowing an arbitrary divisor, or solve the generalized Nash problem.

Overview

An arc is a parametrized curve near a point, described here by two formal power series. Blowing up a point replaces it with an exceptional curve that records directions. A sequence of blowups produces divisors, and each divisor determines a closed set of arcs called its Nash set.

This note varies every free continuation of a fixed initial sequence of centers and computes the arcs belonging to every resulting closed Nash set. Five blowups give intersections that cannot be the claimed contact multiple of any divisor in the fixed reference chain.

The conclusion concerns a specified reference divisor. The same intersections do come from other toric divisors, so the result does not rule out an arbitrary-divisor formulation.

Central result

Work in the centered complex formal arc space 𝒜={(x(t),y(t)):x,y∈tℂ[[t]]}, with ord 0=+∞. The sets below are Zariski-closed sets of arcs, equivalently reduced supports.

For every n≥3 and 2≤k<n, fix the first k centers c₁,…,cₖ of the length-n free chain following y=0. Let 𝓕ₙ,ₖ be the complete family of final prime divisors with that all-free combinatorial type and fixed prefix. In regular coordinates every member is represented by P(x)=Σᵢ₌ₖⁿ⁻¹aᵢxⁱ and y=P(x)+xⁿw, with every coefficient tuple (aₖ,…,aₙ₋₁)∈ℂⁿ⁻ᵏ allowed. This is the entire free family, not a selected subfamily. Smooth curvettas and further free blowups are included; no restriction to minimal embedded resolutions of singular branches is imposed.

For its final divisor E_P, the closed Nash set is N̄_Eₚ={ord x≥1, ord(y−P(x))≥n}. Taking the intersection over all coefficients gives Iₙ,ₖ=⋂_{E′∈𝓕ₙ,ₖ}N̄_E′={ord x≥⌈n/k⌉, ord y≥n}. Requiring exactly k common centers means aₖ≠0 and gives the same closed intersection.

Let Dⱼ be the divisor created at the jth center of the zero reference chain, continued further if necessary. For every positive j and q, the closure of exact-contact-q arcs is Cont̄^q(Dⱼ)={ord x≥q, ord y≥jq}. Closing the at-least-q contact locus gives the same formula.

For n=5,k=2 the intersection is {ord x≥3, ord y≥5}; for n=5,k=3 it is {ord x≥2, ord y≥5}. Neither threshold pair is (q,jq) for any positive integers j,q. The exclusion is for all reference indices and multiplicities, not a bounded computation.

For the specified reference Dₖ, equality Iₙ,ₖ=Cont̄^q(Dₖ) holds exactly when k divides n, with q=n/k. This does not say that every nondivisible pair excludes every other Dⱼ: for example n=6,k=4 gives thresholds (2,6), matching q=2,j=3.

Why the calculation works

Each newest exceptional curve has one point meeting the older exceptional locus. That point is the satellite intersection; all other choices are finite free centers in the displayed polynomial chart. The two final charts are (x,y−P(x))=(x,xⁿw) and (x,y−P(x))=(vh,vⁿ⁻¹hⁿ). They account for the complete family and its satellite limits.

The Nash cylinder is irreducible, and the locus ord x=1 is dense. The deformation xε=x+εt, yε=P(xε)+y−P(x) includes arcs with x=0 and the constant arc in the closure. Raw transverse loci are not substituted for their closed Nash sets.

The two family members P=0 and P=xᵏ force ord y≥n and ord xᵏ≥n; these conditions also suffice for every coefficient tuple. For exactly k common centers, the members xᵏ and 2xᵏ give the same conclusion. Finally, two independent order thresholds agree only when both thresholds agree, so 3j=5 or 2j=5 would be required in the five-blowup examples.

Scope and limitations

The conclusion is about the specified reference multiple under the explicitly treated source conventions. The intersections with weights (3,5) and (2,5) are themselves maximal divisorial sets for other primitive toric divisors. Allowing a different arbitrary divisor removes this particular obstruction. No result about Conjecture 2 or a solution of the generalized Nash problem is claimed.

Equality is equality of closed sets or reduced supports. It is not equality of nonreduced coefficient schemes. The closures include constant arcs, zero-coordinate arcs and satellite limits.

The claim is tied to the inspected arXiv:1501.06898v3 and 2016 workshop formulations. The v3 source defines a relation with “at least i” shared centers but prints an undefined bare subscripted relation in its conjecture, and its selected-point indexing is inconsistent. No unique author-intended correction, erratum or intended new hypothesis is asserted; the publisher-typeset body is not silently identified with that v3.

The note treats the listed prefix, selected-point, indexing and contact readings explicitly. It does not claim to refute an unspecified replacement of the source conjecture. Historical firstness, continuous openness and completeness of the literature search are not established.

Divisible cases can satisfy the reference equality. Fixing the final center gives a singleton divisor. Varying all tangents gives {ord x≥n,ord y≥n}=Cont̄^n(D₁), a positive boundary rather than a counterexample.

The five-blowup examples exclude every reference Dⱼ and positive multiplicity q in each listed reading, including fixing the genuinely free c₃. No unique author-intended correction of the source notation is assumed.

Prior work

The specified-reference assertion comes from Fernández de Bobadilla, Pe Pereira and Popescu-Pampu, On the generalized Nash problem for smooth germs and adjacencies of curve singularities, in the inspected author v3 (2017), and Pe Pereira’s joint-work contribution to Oberwolfach Reports 46/2016, Conjecture 1 on page 2679. Both inspected displays use an intersection.

The maximal-divisorial/contact framework and toric description are established prior work, including Shihoko Ishii’s Maximal divisorial sets in arc spaces. Combinatorial invariance and finite cylindrical intersections are results of the original authors. The contribution here is the complete free-family computation and its obstruction to the reference ray.

The 2018 survey by Fernández de Bobadilla and Pe Pereira discusses the conjectures in Section 8. That historical discussion does not establish present worldwide openness. The original paper’s journal DOI below is a prior-work reference; this note’s own publication DOI is 10.5281/zenodo.23578599.

A projective-line quotient of the Rogalski–Sierra algebra

Alec Kriebel · ORCID 0009-0001-9320-500X · 16 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Original abstract

For the six-relation presentation R(α, β) in Rogalski and Sierra’s 2010 report and 2012 article, the linear ideal (x₃−x₁, x₄−x₂) has a projective-line twisted homogeneous coordinate ring as its exact quotient. It is a nonzero homogeneous completely prime ideal strictly below the augmentation ideal. This gives negative answers to both printed assertions: uniqueness of the nontrivial graded prime and absence of nontrivial maps to twisted homogeneous coordinate rings. The calculation works over every field whenever β²≠1, hence for all the prescribed algebraically independent parameters. The classical twist machinery is credited; historical priority of this explicit quotient remains unresolved.

What the quotient says

A noncommutative algebra can change substantially when two pairs of generators are identified. This note studies one specific identification in the Rogalski–Sierra algebra. The resulting quotient is a familiar twisted coordinate ring of the projective line, with its multiplication written explicitly.

The proof identifies the entire kernel, so the map gives a nonzero completely prime ideal as well as an infinite-dimensional quotient. These supply counterexamples to two literal printed assertions about the original presentation. The construction uses classical machinery, and its historical priority remains unresolved.

The complete result

Let k be any field and let α, β∈k. Give each generator degree one and define the connected graded associative algebra R=R(α,β)=k⟨x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄⟩/(f₁,…,f₆) by the following six quadratic relations. Products are ordered; the second left factor in both f₅ and f₆ is x₄.

f₁=x₁(αx₁−x₃)+x₃(x₁−αx₃); f₂=x₁(αx₂−x₄)+x₃(x₂−αx₄); f₃=x₂(αx₁−x₃)+x₄(x₁−αx₃); f₄=x₂(αx₂−x₄)+x₄(x₂−αx₄); f₅=x₁(βx₁−x₂)+x₄(x₁−βx₂); f₆=x₁(βx₃−x₄)+x₄(x₃−βx₄).

Theorem 1. For every field k, every α∈k and every β∈k with β²≠1, let I=(x₃−x₁,x₄−x₂) be the two-sided ideal and let σ[s:t]=[s+βt:βs+t] on P¹_k. Then R/I≅k⟨X,Y⟩/(βX²−XY+YX−βY²)≅B(P¹_k,O(1),σ). The map sends x₁,x₃ to s and x₂,x₄ to t, and its kernel is exactly I.

The ideal is homogeneous and completely prime, with 0≠I⊊R₊, where R₊ is the augmentation ideal consisting of positive-degree elements. The quotient is a domain for arbitrary elements, so I is both an ordinary prime and a graded prime. Its degree-n dimension is n+1 for every n≥0, its Hilbert series is (1−z)⁻², and its Gelfand–Kirillov dimension is 2.

The twisted homogeneous coordinate ring uses positive pullbacks: Lₙ=O(1)⊗σ⁎O(1)⊗⋯⊗(σⁿ⁻¹)⁎O(1), Bₙ=H⁰(P¹_k,Lₙ), with L₀=O. For f of degree m, multiplication is f⋆g=f⊗(σᵐ)⁎g. The fixed linear lift gives Lₙ≅O(n), and O(1) is σ-ample.

For algebraically independent α,β over the prime subfield of an uncountable algebraically closed field, β²≠1 automatically. The nontrivial prime I contradicts the printed claim that R₊ is the only nontrivial graded prime. The unital graded surjection onto this infinite-dimensional curve ring contradicts the printed claim that no nontrivial homomorphism to a twisted homogeneous coordinate ring exists. Those assertions impose no injectivity, birationality or lower bound on image dimension.

Why the kernel is exact

Substituting x₃=x₁=X and x₄=x₂=Y sends the six defining relations to 0,0,0,0,Q,Q, where Q=βX²−XY+YX−βY². The universal property of free-algebra quotients gives exactly the displayed two-generator quotient. Showing that a relation vanishes in a target would by itself give only a map; the rest of the argument proves there is no additional kernel.

On k[s,t], use the invertible linear automorphism θ(s)=s+βt and θ(t)=βs+t. Its determinant is 1−β². The positive graded twist f⋆g=fθᵐ(g), for f of degree m, is associative, generated in degree one and a domain. It has the same graded vector spaces as the polynomial plane. Its multiplication agrees with the stated projective-line section multiplication.

The relation Q vanishes in this twist, giving a surjection from the two-generator algebra. With U=X−Y and V=Y, the relation becomes VU=((1−β)/(1+β))UV−(β/(1+β))U². Every replacement decreases fixed-length lexicographic order with V>U. Thus the n+1 words UⁱVⁿ⁻ⁱ span degree n. The target already has dimension n+1, so the surjection is an isomorphism in every degree. This proves the exact kernel without assuming confluence or extrapolating from finite rank tables.

There are no linear relations among the four generators of R, so x₃−x₁ is nonzero. The image of x₁ is nonzero, which puts I strictly below R₊. The target domain gives complete primality. Summing the dimensions n+1 gives cumulative dimension (n+1)(n+2)/2 and the stated growth.

Scope and boundaries

The all-field statement concerns the displayed six-relation presentation. In characteristic different from two, the geometric parameter changes c=(ϑ−1)/(ϑ+1) and d=(ρ−1)/(ρ+1) preserve the independent-parameter setting. In characteristic two these fractions collapse to 1 when defined. The independent-parameter characteristic-two presentation is not thereby identified with that geometric family, and the latter’s noetherianity or GK-dimension-four conclusions are not transferred through the collapse.

The condition β²≠1 is essential: at β=±1, Q factors as (X+Y)(X−Y) or −(X−Y)(X+Y), giving nonzero linear zero divisors. The allowed value β=0 gives the commutative polynomial plane. The change U=X−Y,V=Y and the proof do not require division by 2 or infinite automorphism order.

This is a quotient map with a nonzero kernel. It does not claim an injective or birational map, a classification of all primes, or equality of the graded quotient rings of the source surface algebra and a twisted homogeneous coordinate ring. The separate same-graded-quotient-ring surface obstruction is unaffected by this curve quotient.

Historical priority remains unresolved. Comparisons use selected primary passages and specified preprint versions; the original Artin–Van den Bergh body, some final journal editions, parts of the Campbell thesis and broader older or unindexed literature were not all inspected. No firstness, exhaustive predecessor absence or present worldwide-open status is claimed.

Classical context and priority

The two assertions and the literal six-relation presentation occur in Sierra’s 2010 Oberwolfach contribution with Rogalski and in Rogalski–Sierra’s 2012 article. Their specific formulas, including the x₄ factors in f₅ and f₆, are part of the statement addressed here. The contribution recorded by this note is the explicit substitution and exact projective-line quotient.

Twisted homogeneous coordinate rings are the classical construction of Artin and Van den Bergh. Polynomial graded twists, the associated quantum/Jordan or Ore-plane descriptions and degree-reduction arguments are also classical. These ingredients and the Rogalski–Zhang canonical-map machinery retain their prior credit.

Strong noetherianity is a sufficient hypothesis of Rogalski–Zhang’s main canonical-map theorem. Their broader Theorem 4.4 provides another route using subexponential growth and eventual stabilization of point-module truncation maps. Strong noetherianity is therefore not the only route in that work. The required stabilization hypotheses have not been established here for the source algebra merely by citation.

Nevins–Sierra’s point-tail and geometric results have their own moduli and dimension hypotheses, and a universal canonical factor need not itself be a twisted homogeneous coordinate ring. Repetitions of the contrary no-map assertion are attributed to the inspected arXiv v1 and v2 preprints, rather than an unread final journal body. Selected Campbell thesis results on infinitesimal deformations and function skew fields concern a distinct deformation family; they are credited without claiming an exhaustive thesis or literature search.

Read the paper

Read the complete unchanged four-page version 1.0 paper below, or open or download the PDF. The complete original source and verification ZIP preserves the authored companion materials and original archives. Its README gives requirements and distinctions between the core and optional controls; third-party primary bodies are not included.

Research

A Robinson counterexample to ideal-only tangency certificates

Alec Kriebel · ORCID

12 October 2026 · Version 1.0 · Unrefereed preprint

Original abstract

The classical Robinson sextic is nonnegative, but adding any nonnegative constant does not make it a sum of polynomial squares modulo the ideal of polynomials vanishing on its real tangency variety. This rules out both the exact radical certificate and the positive-constant certificate in the proposed unrestricted replacement of the gradient ideal. The same obstruction applies to the separate-cross-product ideal printed in the original report. Ten zero lines force the low-degree homogeneous parts of all square summands to vanish; an additional coordinate axis then makes the certificate impossible. The proof allows arbitrarily many summands of arbitrary degree and is entirely elementary. We credit the classical form and zero-set method, and make no claim of first bibliographic priority.

What the result means

A sum of real polynomial squares is always nonnegative. One way to certify that a polynomial is nonnegative is to express it as such a sum, allowing an additional polynomial that vanishes on a chosen set. The choice of that set matters.

This note applies Robinson’s classical sextic to two proposed ideal-only certificates. The polynomial is nonnegative everywhere, yet neither certificate works, even after adding any nonnegative constant. The obstruction permits any finite number of square summands with arbitrary real coefficients and arbitrary finite degrees. It is not a failure found by searching only up to a degree cutoff.

The full result

Work in S=ℝ[x,y,z]. For a polynomial f, write f_x, f_y and f_z for its partial derivatives. Define the two ideals separately:

J_f=(y f_x−x f_y, z f_x−x f_z, z f_y−y f_z). K_f=(y f_x, x f_y, z f_x, x f_z, z f_y, y f_z).

For an ideal L, V_ℝ(L) is the set of real points where every polynomial in L vanishes. Let I_ℝ(L) be the full ideal of all real polynomials vanishing on that set, and let ΣS² denote finite sums of squares of real polynomials. The ordinary radical satisfies L⊆√L⊆I_ℝ(L).

The Robinson sextic is R=x⁶+y⁶+z⁶−x⁴y²−x²y⁴−x⁴z²−x²z⁴−y⁴z²−y²z⁴+3x²y²z².

Theorem 1. R is nonnegative on all of ℝ³. For both L=J_R and L=K_R and every real ε≥0, R+ε ∉ ΣS²+I_ℝ(L).

Equivalently, there are no finite m, real polynomials q₁,…,q_m of arbitrary degrees, and h∈I_ℝ(L) with R+ε=∑q_j²+h. No fixed degree bound or bound on the finite summand count is imposed. The theorem includes ε=0 and every positive constant.

Consequently R∉ΣS²+√L, and R+ε∉ΣS²+L for every ε>0, for each of the two ideals. Thus global nonnegativity does not imply either proposed ideal-only certificate. R attains its minimum zero; removing an attainment assumption includes attained examples.

Tangency-minor nonnegativity equivalence. For every real polynomial f in n≥1 variables, nonnegativity on ℝⁿ is equivalent to nonnegativity on the real variety of the minors x_j f_{x_i}−x_i f_{x_j}. No global minimum-attainment or bounded-infimum hypothesis is needed. A negative value away from the origin produces a negative minimum on a compact sphere, where the gradient is parallel to the radius; the origin itself always belongs to the variety. For n=1 there are no minors and the variety is the whole line.

Separate-product diagnostic. In two variables let Q(x,y)=(1−xy)²+y²−1/2 and K_Q=(y Q_x,x Q_y). Then V_ℝ(K_Q)={(0,0)}, where Q=1/2, although Q(2,1/2)=−1/4. Its infimum −1/2 is not attained, since equality would require both y=0 and xy=1; Q(1/u,u)=u²−1/2 approaches that infimum. This is a constant shift of a standard nonattaining example. It concerns only the separate-product reading and does not contradict the tangency-minor equivalence.

Why the obstruction works

The nonnegativity is a classical Schur calculation. Put a=x², b=y² and c=z². The symmetric expression for R can be written as (a−b)²(a+b−c)+c(a−c)(b−c). After ordering a≥b≥c≥0, both terms are nonnegative.

The ten directions (1,s,t), (1,s,0), (1,0,t) and (0,1,t), with each applicable sign independently equal to ±1, give ten whole zero lines of R. Each line lies in both real varieties because the gradient vanishes at every global minimizer. The coordinate axis (u,0,0) also lies in both varieties, and R(u,0,0)=u⁶.

Suppose a certificate existed. On a zero line it would give ε=∑q_j(uv)² for every real u. Each restricted polynomial is bounded and therefore constant. The classical ten-zero cubic argument then forces every square summand’s homogeneous parts of degrees one, two and three to vanish identically. Its constant part is retained; for positive ε it need not be zero.

On the coordinate axis the same certificate gives u⁶+ε=∑q_j(u,0,0)². A restriction of degree above three would contribute a strictly positive highest coefficient that cannot cancel with the other real squares. Thus every restriction has degree at most three. The already-vanishing low-degree parts make every restriction constant, contradicting u⁶+ε. This handles arbitrary finite degrees without assuming the whole variety is finite or the original ideal is radical.

The complete supporting archive contains the manuscript source, authored verification materials and preserved review history. Exact algebra checks accompany the elementary universal proof; neither numerical solver failure nor a fixed sum-of-squares degree cutoff proves the nonexistence claim.

Scope and limitations

The negative statement concerns finite sums of squares of real polynomials plus the specified ideal remainder. It is not a claim about rational-function, complex, analytic or infinite-sum certificates. It makes no negative claim about stronger models with added inequalities or sum-of-squares multipliers.

The ordinary gradient ideal is different: Euler’s identity gives 6R=x R_x+y R_y+z R_z, so R already belongs to (R_x,R_y,R_z). The example does not refute the attained-minimum gradient-ideal theorem.

The printed Oberwolfach formula uses separate products, while the tangency-minor ideal is treated as a separately explicit formulation. No uniquely intended or author-approved correction of the printed formula is asserted, and no current catalogue status is inferred.

Historical first priority and continued worldwide openness are not established. Complete original 2008 and 2009 Hà–Pham article texts were not obtained for the source comparison; related truncated-certificate comparisons use later primary statements and retain their extra multiplier terms. The inspected Schweighofer author preprint is not silently identified with an unread final SIAM journal body.

Background and credit

Robinson’s nonnegative sextic, Schur’s inequality and the zero-set method are classical. Reznick’s 2000 published reprint, Section 4(b), printed pages 258–259, gives the same form, ten zero directions and cubic obstruction. The note’s contribution is their explicit application to both ideal-only certificates, using whole zero lines and an additional axis to include every nonnegative constant.

In Oberwolfach Report 14/2007, Schweighofer’s Theorem 1 on printed page 810 states the gradient-ideal equivalence with a minimum-attainment assumption. Conjecture 2 on printed page 811 proposes removing that assumption with a displayed separate-product replacement. The note evaluates that literal product ideal and the separately defined tangency-minor ideal; it does not silently replace one by the other. Robinson’s form already appears in Reznick’s contribution to the same report, printed page 798, equation (2).

The sphere-minimization mechanism is credited to the standard argument also used in Laurent’s updated manuscript dated 6 February 2010, Section 7.2.3, Lemma 7.21, manuscript pages 117–118. That locator belongs to the updated manuscript, rather than the differently numbered lemma in the earlier 2009 chapter. Schweighofer’s gradient-tentacle certificates and the truncated/generalized-critical-value certificates of Hà–Pham and Guo–Safey El Din–Zhi use additional inequalities or SOS multipliers and remain distinct from this ideal-only obstruction.

Contribution and collaboration

Independent mathematical verification, a substantive connection to stronger positivity certificates, or mathematical and expository work toward a journal version would be welcome. Any collaboration and authorship would reflect actual scholarly contributions.

AI and review disclosure

AI tools were used extensively in developing, checking and presenting the argument, including literature review, computation, adversarial review and writing. This is an unrefereed preprint without independent human or journal peer review. Internal AI-assisted checks are not human review, and no formal proof-assistant certification is claimed.

records.full_original_abstract: The classical Robinson sextic is nonnegative, but adding any nonnegative constant does not make it a sum of polynomial squares modulo the ideal of polynomials vanishing on its real tangency variety. This rules out both the exact radical certificate and the positive-constant certificate in the proposed unrestricted replacement of the gradient ideal. The same obstruction applies to the separate-cross-product ideal printed in the original report. Ten zero lines force the low-degree homogeneous parts of all square summands to vanish; an additional coordinate axis then makes the certificate impossible. The proof allows arbitrarily many summands of arbitrary degree and is entirely elementary. We credit the classical form and zero-set method, and make no claim of first bibliographic priority.
